text:
On February 12, 1966, Barbara Weiss wore her good shoes to synagogue because the other pair pinched, and because she had been told walking was good for the baby. The baby, who had not yet agreed to be born, pressed its heels beneath her ribs as she made her way through the snow.

The synagogue stood in Southfield, which people still called Detroit when talking to relatives in New York. Its lobby smelled of wet wool, floor wax, and coffee kept warm in a silver urn. Barbara’s husband, David, had dropped her at the entrance and gone to find a parking space. They had been married four years, still at the stage when a promise about parking could be taken as a promise about the world.

Barbara was thirty-one weeks pregnant. Her coat would not close, so she fastened it with a brass pin that had belonged to her mother. People kept telling her she looked well. She had begun to hear it as a kind of weather report: the sky is cloudy, you look well, there may be a child by spring.

Rabbi Adler was speaking about Abraham. He was renowned, though Barbara thought the word sounded ridiculous applied to someone she had watched make a face at the sputtering coffee urn. He was known beyond Detroit and had appeared on television twice. His sermons were collected in a blue book her father kept beside the encyclopedia.

The rabbi had a way of making old stories seem less old than the people listening to them. Barbara sat near the aisle, where she could stretch her legs. She watched the backs of heads: Mr. Cohen’s bald patch, a girl’s braid, David’s dark hair two rows ahead. The baby rolled, and Barbara rested a hand over the movement.

Then a young man stood.

Barbara first thought he was trying to leave. People stood during services for ordinary reasons: to let someone pass, find a child, escape a cough. The man was thin and pale, his hair falling over his forehead. His suit seemed borrowed. He looked toward the rabbi, but not quite at him, as if he were looking beyond him.

The first shot seemed, for a fraction of a second, to belong to the service. It was too loud, so the mind tried to place it somewhere else: a slammed door, a dropped tray. Then Rabbi Adler fell, and the sanctuary broke open.

More shots followed. People ducked, screamed, climbed over pews. Someone knocked Barbara’s shoulder; someone else grabbed her sleeve. The young man turned the gun on himself and fell near the front. Beneath the noise came a terrible stillness, as if the room were asking everyone to explain what had happened.

Barbara had seen his face. That was what she remembered most clearly, though for years she tried to recall other things instead: the stained glass, someone’s perfume, the exact words of the sermon. The young man had looked frightened. Not furious or triumphant, but frightened in the plain human way Barbara felt when she woke at night and could not tell whether the baby had moved.

She stood up.

She meant to go to him. She did not know what she would do when she got there. Later, she imagined she might have spoken to him, taken the gun, or put her coat around his shoulders. She had those thoughts because she could not bear to believe she had had no thought at all.

But the crowd moved toward the exits as a body, not as a collection of people. An elbow struck her stomach. Someone shouted there might be another gunman. Barbara was pushed sideways, then backward, her feet dragged across the carpet. She tried to hold a pew, but a hand caught her wrist and pulled. The brass pin sprang loose. Her coat fell open. One hand over her belly, the other reaching toward a room she could no longer see, she was carried outside.

Snow had begun again. David was running from the parking lot. He saw her, called her name, and caught her before she fell. People spilled from the synagogue behind him, crying, silent, or still unsure whether to run farther. A woman in a blue scarf kept saying, “The rabbi, the rabbi,” as if the words could summon him back.

David held Barbara against him. She was shivering, though the cold had not started it. He kept asking if she was hurt. She said no. She said the baby was moving. She said she had to go back.

“You can’t,” he said.

“He was just a boy.”

David looked at her, then at the building. He did not ask which boy. They had both seen him.

At the hospital, the baby was judged healthy. Barbara was given a blanket and told to lie still. David sat beside her, rubbing his wedding ring with his thumb. The doctors spoke practically: her body was not in danger; the baby’s heartbeat was good; there was no reason to think the shock had caused harm. The world, in their account, had procedures and outcomes. It was useful to hear, though it did not make the world seem orderly.

That night she dreamed of the sanctuary. The young man stood at the front, but the rabbi sat in his usual chair. Barbara walked down the aisle and asked the young man if he needed help. He said no. She asked again, because she had not heard him. Then the baby kicked so hard that she woke.

The newspapers gave the young man a name. They said he had been a student, then qualified what that meant. They described him as troubled and quoted people who had known him, and people who had not. The rabbi’s life filled careful paragraphs: his childhood, education, years in Detroit, books, and work with young people. The young man’s life took less space. For days, the papers printed a photograph in which he looked even younger than he had in the synagogue.

Barbara read everything, looking for some detail that would make his face intelligible. There was none. He had been lonely, one person said; intelligent, said another. Angry. Quiet. People spoke with the confidence of those who wanted a conclusion.

The rabbi was buried. Barbara did not attend the funeral. Her doctor advised her to stay home, and David insisted she obey. She spent the morning by a window overlooking the driveway as snow slid from the roof in thin sheets. Her mother called and asked whether she was managing. Barbara said she was. Asked if she was frightened, she answered, “Not exactly.” It was the truest answer she could give.

Their daughter was born in April. They named her Ruth, after David’s grandmother, who had survived a war and disliked being called brave. Barbara held the baby and was surprised by the strength of her small hands. Birth was not an arrival, something that happened to a household. It was a demand, immediate and direct. Ruth wanted warmth, milk, a clean cloth. She did not care that a rabbi had died or that a young man had killed him, or that Barbara had tried and failed to cross a room.

For a while, Barbara was grateful for that. The baby gave her tasks small enough to complete. Later, when Ruth was old enough to ask why her mother sometimes went quiet at a sudden bang, Barbara told her there had been a terrible day at the synagogue. She did not say she had tried to reach the shooter. She could not explain the impulse without making it sound nobler than it was. Nor could she explain the shame she felt at being swept out with everyone else.

Years passed. David’s hair thinned. Ruth grew tall, learned to drive, and left Michigan for college. The synagogue renovated its sanctuary. The carpet was replaced, the chairs rearranged, and the old coffee urn discarded. Rabbi Adler’s name remained on a plaque by the entrance. People brought their children to services and pointed it out in the quiet manner reserved for the dead.

Barbara still attended. She did not want to make a monument of that morning. When people who had heard the story secondhand asked what it had been like, she usually said, “Confusing.” It was accurate, and discouraged further questions.

One winter afternoon, many years later, she found the brass pin in a sewing box beneath a packet of buttons. She held it in her palm and remembered the crowd’s pressure, her torn sleeve, the sanctuary lights. Most of all she remembered the young man’s face—not because she believed she had understood him, but because she had not. Fear had looked back at her from the front of the room, and she had wanted to cross the distance.

She put the pin in a drawer beside the spare keys. Outside, snow began to fall, light enough at first to be mistaken for dust. She watched it gather on the sill, then turned on the kitchen light. There was dinner to make. There always had been, in the years after. It was not forgiveness, an answer, or the end of remembering. It was simply what came next.
